fr:mainmatter.html:p: A topological space X is first-countable if every point x\in X has an at most countable local basis. It is second-countable if its topology has an at most countable basis.

These conditions constrain two different scales. First-countability gives a countable collection of tests near each individual point, while second-countability gives one countable collection of basic open sets for the whole space.

General topology studies the structures that remain after distance, angle, and coordinates have been forgotten. What remains is a rule for deciding which subsets are open. From this rule one can recover a useful notion of nearness, formulate continuity without a metric, and compare spaces up to homeomorphism. The resulting language is broad enough to treat Euclidean spaces, function spaces, quotient constructions, and spaces that cannot be described by distances at all.

This note follows the order and conventions of the general-topology part of Munkres's Topology, with occasional comparison to the Stacks Project topology chapter. In particular, compactness means the finite-subcover property and does not include Hausdorffness.

A topology does not assign a numerical distance to two points. Instead, it records which collections of points may serve as observable regions. The three topology axioms say that these regions include the trivial ones and are stable under the unions and finite intersections needed to combine observations.

A topology on a set X is a collection \tau \subseteq \mathcal {P}(X) satisfying the following axioms:
\varnothing \in \tau and X\in \tau .
If \{U_i\}_{i\in I}\subseteq \tau , then \bigcup _{i\in I}U_i\in \tau .
If U_1,\ldots ,U_n\in \tau , then U_1\cap \cdots \cap U_n\in \tau . The pair (X,\tau ) is a topological space, and the members of \tau are its open sets. A subset F\subseteq X is closed when X\setminus F is open; it is clopen when it is both open and closed.

Let \tau _1 and \tau _2 be topologies on the same set X. The topology \tau _1 is finer, or stronger, than \tau _2 if
\tau _2\subseteq \tau _1.
Equivalently, \tau _2 is coarser, or weaker, than \tau _1. Thus a finer topology has more open sets and imposes a stronger continuity requirement on maps into the space.

Open sets describe the space globally. Near one fixed point it is more economical to work with neighborhoods, and for the entire topology it is often enough to specify a basis. These two reductions will later control continuity, countability, and product constructions.

Let X be a topological space and let x\in X. A subset N\subseteq X is a neighborhood of x if there is an open set U such that
x\in U\subseteq N.
In particular, a neighborhood need not itself be open.

A collection \mathcal {B}_x of neighborhoods of x is a local basis at x if every neighborhood N of x contains some B\in \mathcal {B}_x. A statement holds locally at x when it holds on some neighborhood of x.

Let (X,\tau ) be a topological space. A collection \mathcal {B}\subseteq \tau is a basis for \tau if, whenever U\in \tau and x\in U, there is some B\in \mathcal {B} such that
x\in B\subseteq U.
Equivalently, every open set is a union of members of \mathcal {B}.

A collection \mathcal {B}\subseteq \mathcal {P}(X) generates a topology by taking arbitrary unions of its members provided that it covers X and satisfies the refinement condition
x\in B_1\cap B_2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \exists B_3\in \mathcal {B},\; x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2.

A single set can carry many topologies. At the two extremes, the discrete topology declares every subset open, whereas the indiscrete topology retains only the opens forced by the axioms. Euclidean topology and, on an infinite set, cofinite topology provide less degenerate examples between these extremes.

Let X be a set. The discrete topology on X is the power set \mathcal {P}(X), so every subset is open. The indiscrete topology is \{\varnothing ,X\}, so only the two sets required by the topology axioms are open.
These are respectively the finest and coarsest topologies on the fixed underlying set X.

For n\geq 1, let
d(x,y)=\sqrt {\sum _{i=1}^{n}(x_i-y_i)^2}
be the Euclidean distance on \mathbb {R}^n. A subset U\subseteq \mathbb {R}^n is Euclidean open if, for every x\in U, there is some \varepsilon >0 such that
B_\varepsilon (x) =\{y\in \mathbb {R}^n\mid d(x,y)<\varepsilon \} \subseteq U.
The collection of Euclidean open subsets is the Euclidean topology on \mathbb {R}^n.
When n=1, the open balls are open intervals. Thus a subset U\subseteq \mathbb {R} is Euclidean open precisely when every x\in U lies in an interval (a,b)\subseteq U.
Let X be a set. The cofinite topology on X consists of \varnothing together with every subset U\subseteq X whose complement X\setminus U is finite.

Once spaces have been specified, the appropriate maps between them are those that respect open sets. The preimage formulation is deliberately asymmetric: it works for every function, preserves unions and intersections, and therefore composes without additional hypotheses.

Let (X,\tau _X) and (Y,\tau _Y) be topological spaces. A map f:X\to Y is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open:
V\in \tau _Y \quad \Longrightarrow \quad f^{-1}(V)\in \tau _X.
Equivalently, the preimage of every closed subset of Y is closed in X. Continuity therefore depends on both the underlying function and the topologies placed on its domain and codomain.
Let \mathcal {B} be a basis for the topology of Y. A map f:X\to Y is continuous if and only if f^{-1}(B) is open in X for every B\in \mathcal {B}.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The forward implication follows immediately from continuity because every basis element is open. Conversely, suppose the preimage of each basis element is open. Every open subset V\subseteq Y is a union of basis elements, say V=\bigcup _{i\in I}B_i. Preimages preserve arbitrary unions, so
f^{-1}(V) =f^{-1}\left (\bigcup _{i\in I}B_i\right ) =\bigcup _{i\in I}f^{-1}(B_i).
The right-hand side is open in X; hence f is continuous.

fr:title.text: Identity and Composition of Continuous Maps

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Identity and Composition of Continuous Maps

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The identity map on every topological space is continuous. If f:X\to Y and g:Y\to Z are continuous maps, then their composite g\circ f:X\to Z is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
For every open set U\subseteq X, one has \operatorname {id}_X^{-1}(U)=U, so the identity is continuous. If W\subseteq Z is open, then
(g\circ f)^{-1}(W)=f^{-1}\left (g^{-1}(W)\right ).
Continuity of g makes g^{-1}(W) open in Y, and continuity of f then makes its preimage open in X.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Continuity belongs to a map together with its domain and codomain topologies; it is not merely a property of the underlying formula. The identity between two differently topologized copies of the same set is the smallest example where this dependence becomes visible.

Put the Euclidean topology \tau _e and the cofinite topology \tau _c on the same underlying set \mathbb {R}. The identity function
\operatorname {id}:(\mathbb {R},\tau _e) \longrightarrow (\mathbb {R},\tau _c)
is continuous. Indeed, the complement of every cofinite open set is finite. Singletons are Euclidean closed, and finite unions of closed sets remain closed, so every cofinite open set is Euclidean open.

The identity in the reverse direction is not continuous. The interval (0,1) is Euclidean open, but its preimage under the identity is not cofinite open because \mathbb {R}\setminus (0,1) is infinite. Thus the same set-theoretic function can be continuous in one direction and discontinuous in the other.

A homeomorphism is the topological analogue of an isomorphism. It permits information to move continuously in both directions, so every property expressed solely in terms of the topology is preserved.

A homeomorphism between topological spaces X and Y is a bijective continuous map f:X\to Y whose inverse f^{-1}:Y\to X is also continuous. If such a map exists, X and Y are homeomorphic, written X\cong Y.

A continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism: continuity controls preimages of open sets, whereas continuity of the inverse also requires the original map to preserve the topology in the opposite direction.

fr:title.text: The Real Line and an Open Interval Are Homeomorphic

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Real Line and an Open Interval Are Homeomorphic

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
The map
f:\mathbb {R}\longrightarrow (0,1), \qquad f(x)=\frac 12+\frac {1}{\pi }\arctan x
is a bijection. It is continuous, and its inverse
f^{-1}(t)=\tan \left (\pi \left (t-\frac 12\right )\right )
is continuous on (0,1). Hence f is a homeomorphism. Topologically, boundedness and total length do not distinguish the open interval from the whole real line.

Three constructions account for a large fraction of naturally occurring spaces. A subset inherits opens from an ambient space, a product is observed through its coordinate projections, and a quotient is obtained by identifying points. Their definitions are best read together using the comparison of topologies: subspace and product topologies are the coarsest topologies making the relevant maps continuous, while the quotient topology is the finest one detected by the quotient map.
Passing to a subspace changes the ambient meaning of openness. An endpoint can acquire an open one-sided neighborhood even though no such set is open in the real line itself.

fr:title.text: Universal Property of the Subspace Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Universal Property of the Subspace Topology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let A\subseteq X carry the subspace topology, and let \iota :A\hookrightarrow X be the inclusion. A map f:Z\to A is continuous if and only if \iota \circ f:Z\to X is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The inclusion is continuous: for every open U\subseteq X, its preimage is A\cap U, which is open in A. Thus the forward implication follows from closure under composition.
Conversely, suppose \iota \circ f is continuous. Every open subset of A has the form A\cap U for some open U\subseteq X, and
f^{-1}(A\cap U)=(\iota \circ f)^{-1}(U).
This set is open in Z, so f is continuous.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Give A=[0,1] the subspace topology inherited from the real line. Then the subset
\{x\in A\mid 0\leq x<1\}=A\cap (-1,1)
is open in A, although it is not open in \mathbb {R}. Likewise, \{x\in A\mid 0<x\leq 1\} is open in A. The word open therefore always refers to an ambient topological space.

The product topology permits observations in finitely many coordinates at a time. This finite-coordinate condition is invisible for ordinary finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces but is essential for infinite products.

Let \{X_i\}_{i\in I} be a family of topological spaces. The product topology on the Cartesian product \prod _{i\in I}X_i has as a basis the sets
\prod _{i\in I}U_i,
where each U_i is open in X_i and U_i=X_i for all but finitely many indices i. Equivalently, it is the coarsest topology that makes every coordinate projection
\pi _i:\prod _{j\in I}X_j\longrightarrow X_i
continuous.

For a finite product X_1\times \cdots \times X_n, the basic open sets are simply products U_1\times \cdots \times U_n of open sets. For an infinite product, the finite-coordinate restriction distinguishes the product topology from the generally finer box topology.

fr:title.text: Universal Property of the Product Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Universal Property of the Product Topology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X=\prod _{i\in I}X_i carry the product topology, with projections \pi _i:X\to X_i. A map f:Z\to X is continuous if and only if every coordinate map \pi _i\circ f:Z\to X_i is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
If f is continuous, each coordinate map is continuous because the projections are continuous. Conversely, suppose all coordinate maps are continuous. Every basic open subset of X can be written as
B=\bigcap _{k=1}^{n}\pi _{i_k}^{-1}(U_{i_k}),
where each U_{i_k} is open in X_{i_k}. Therefore
f^{-1}(B) =\bigcap _{k=1}^{n}(\pi _{i_k}\circ f)^{-1}(U_{i_k}),
a finite intersection of open subsets of Z. The basis criterion now shows that f is continuous.

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
For positive integers m,n, the coordinate-concatenation bijection
\mathbb {R}^m\times \mathbb {R}^n \longrightarrow \mathbb {R}^{m+n}, \qquad (x,y)\longmapsto (x_1,\ldots ,x_m,y_1,\ldots ,y_n)
is a homeomorphism from the product of the Euclidean topologies to the Euclidean topology on \mathbb {R}^{m+n}.

Around a point (x,y), Euclidean balls and products of Euclidean balls refine one another. More precisely,
B_{\frac {\varepsilon }{\sqrt {2}}}(x)\times B_{\frac {\varepsilon }{\sqrt {2}}}(y) \subseteq B_\varepsilon (x,y) \subseteq B_\varepsilon (x)\times B_\varepsilon (y).
The two sides therefore generate the same open neighborhoods.

A quotient reverses the direction of construction. Instead of restricting an existing topology, it asks which subsets of the target can be recognized as open after pulling them back to the source. Its universal property is the practical way to construct maps out of a quotient.

Let X be a topological space and let q:X\to Y be a surjection. The quotient topology on Y is defined by
U\subseteq Y\text { is open} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad q^{-1}(U)\text { is open in }X.
With this topology, q is called a quotient map. It is the finest topology on Y for which q is continuous.

In particular, if \sim is an equivalence relation on X, the canonical surjection
q:X\longrightarrow X/{\sim }, \qquad x\longmapsto [x]
equips the quotient set X/{\sim } with a topology. The resulting topological space is the quotient space of X by \sim .

fr:title.text: Universal Property of the Quotient Topology

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Universal Property of the Quotient Topology

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let q:X\to Y be a quotient map. For every topological space Z, a map g:Y\to Z is continuous if and only if g\circ q:X\to Z is continuous.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
If g is continuous, then g\circ q is continuous by closure under composition. Conversely, suppose g\circ q is continuous and let W\subseteq Z be open. Then
q^{-1}\left (g^{-1}(W)\right ) =(g\circ q)^{-1}(W)
is open in X. The defining property of the quotient topology implies that g^{-1}(W) is open in Y. Hence g is continuous.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Connectedness asks whether a space can be decomposed into two open pieces without overlap. This is a global property: every sufficiently small portion of a space may look simple while the whole space still splits into disconnected pieces.
A separation of a topological space X is a pair of disjoint, nonempty open sets U,V\subseteq X such that X=U\cup V. The space X is connected if it admits no separation.
Equivalently, X is connected precisely when its only clopen subsets are \varnothing and X. In this note the empty space is regarded as connected, since it has no separation.
The least-upper-bound property of the real numbers prevents an interval from splitting at an omitted boundary point. This supplies the basic source of connected examples in analysis.

fr:title.text: Intervals in the Real Line Are Connected

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Intervals in the Real Line Are Connected

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let I\subseteq \mathbb {R} be an interval: whenever a,b\in I and a<c<b, one also has c\in I. Then I, with the Euclidean subspace topology, is connected.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Suppose instead that I=U\cup V is a separation. Choose u\in U and v\in V; after exchanging the names if necessary, assume u<v. The interval property gives [u,v]\subseteq I. Set
S=U\cap [u,v], \qquad c=\sup S.
The supremum exists by the least-upper-bound property, and u\leq c\leq v, so c\in I.
The point c cannot lie in U. If c<v, openness of U in I would place points of U\cap [u,v] strictly above c, contradicting the definition of the supremum. If c=v, then membership in U would contradict v\in V and U\cap V=\varnothing . Hence c\in V.
Since V is open in I, some \varepsilon >0 satisfies
(c-\varepsilon ,c+\varepsilon )\cap I\subseteq V.
By the defining property of the supremum, there is some s\in S with c-\varepsilon <s\leq c. Since c\notin U, in fact s<c. But then s\in U\cap V, a contradiction. Thus no separation exists.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The next theorem makes connectedness useful under constructions. A continuous map may collapse points, but it cannot tear one connected space into a disconnected image.
If X is connected and f:X\to Y is continuous, then the image f(X), with its subspace topology, is connected.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
First regard f as a map \bar f:X\to f(X). This corestriction is continuous: if U=f(X)\cap O is open in the subspace f(X), with O open in Y, then
\bar f^{-1}(U)=f^{-1}(O),
which is open in X.
Suppose f(X)=U\cup V were a separation. Continuity of \bar f makes \bar f^{-1}(U) and \bar f^{-1}(V) open in X. They are disjoint and cover X; they are also nonempty because \bar f is surjective. They would therefore form a separation of X, contradicting connectedness.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Compactness replaces an arbitrary amount of local covering data by a finite amount. It is a topological finiteness condition, not a statement about numerical boundedness. Closed bounded intervals motivate the definition, but the definition continues to make sense in every topological space.

An open cover of a topological space X is a collection \mathcal {U} of open subsets such that
X=\bigcup _{U\in \mathcal {U}}U.
A finite subcover is a finite subcollection \mathcal {V}\subseteq \mathcal {U} such that
X=\bigcup _{V\in \mathcal {V}}V.
The finite subcollection may be empty.
The space X is compact if every open cover of X has a finite subcover. A subset K\subseteq X is compact when it is compact with its subspace topology.

Following Munkres, compactness here does not include the Hausdorff condition. Some texts call this property quasi-compactness and reserve compact for Hausdorff spaces with the finite-subcover property.

fr:title.text: Closed Intervals in the Real Line Are Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Closed Intervals in the Real Line Are Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For real numbers a\leq b, the closed interval [a,b]\subseteq \mathbb {R} is compact in the Euclidean topology.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The case a=b is immediate. Assume a<b, and let \mathcal {U} be an open cover of [a,b]. Define
S=\{x\in [a,b]\mid [a,x]\text { is covered by finitely many members of } \mathcal {U}\}.
A member of the cover containing a also contains a short interval to the right of a, so S is nonempty. It is bounded above by b; let c=\sup S, using the least-upper-bound property.
Suppose c<b. Choose U\in \mathcal {U} containing c. Since U is open in the subspace [a,b], some \varepsilon >0 satisfies
(c-\varepsilon ,c+\varepsilon )\cap [a,b]\subseteq U.
Choose x\in S with c-\frac {\varepsilon }{2}<x\leq c. A finite cover of [a,x], together with U, covers [a,y] for some y>c. This places y in S, contradicting that c is an upper bound. Hence c=b.
Finally choose a member of the cover containing b. For some \delta >0, it contains every x\in [a,b] satisfying b-\delta <x\leq b. Since b=\sup S, choose x\in S with b-\delta <x\leq b. A finite cover of [a,x] together with this last member covers all of [a,b]. Therefore every open cover has a finite subcover.

fr:title.text: Closed Subspaces of Compact Spaces Are Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Closed Subspaces of Compact Spaces Are Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every closed subspace A of a compact space X is compact.
If X is compact and f:X\to Y is continuous, then the image f(X), with its subspace topology, is compact.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Regard f as a map \bar f:X\to f(X). It is continuous because the preimage of a subspace-open set f(X)\cap O is f^{-1}(O), which is open in X.
Let \mathcal {U} be an open cover of f(X). The collection
\{\bar f^{-1}(U)\mid U\in \mathcal {U}\}
is an open cover of X. Choose a finite subcover \bar f^{-1}(U_1),\ldots ,\bar f^{-1}(U_n). Surjectivity of \bar f then implies that U_1,\ldots ,U_n covers f(X).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Hausdorffness and compactness do not imply one another. Hausdorffness requires distinct points to admit disjoint observations and thereby rules out several pathologies of coarse topologies. It passes to subspaces and products, though an arbitrary quotient of a Hausdorff space need not remain Hausdorff.

A topological space X is Hausdorff, or T_2, if any two distinct points can be separated by disjoint open neighborhoods. That is, for x,y\in X with x\neq y, there are open sets U,V\subseteq X such that
x\in U,\qquad y\in V,\qquad U\cap V=\varnothing .
Every subspace of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff, and every product of Hausdorff spaces is Hausdorff in the product topology.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let A\subseteq X, where X is Hausdorff, and choose distinct points x,y\in A. Disjoint open neighborhoods U,V\subseteq X of x and y restrict to disjoint open neighborhoods A\cap U and A\cap V in A. Thus A is Hausdorff.
Now let X=\prod _{i\in I}X_i, with every X_i Hausdorff, and choose distinct points x,y\in X. They differ in some coordinate i. Choose disjoint open neighborhoods U_i,V_i\subseteq X_i of x_i and y_i. Their inverse images \pi _i^{-1}(U_i) and \pi _i^{-1}(V_i) are disjoint open neighborhoods of x and y in X.

fr:title.text: Compact Subsets of Hausdorff Spaces Are Closed

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Compact Subsets of Hausdorff Spaces Are Closed

fr:mainmatter.html:p: If K is a compact subspace of a Hausdorff space X, then K is closed in X.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
The empty subset is closed, so suppose K is nonempty. Fix x\in X\setminus K. For each y\in K, choose disjoint open sets U_y and V_y with y\in U_y and x\in V_y. The sets K\cap U_y form an open cover of the subspace K; compactness gives finitely many indices y_1,\ldots ,y_n for which U_{y_1},\ldots ,U_{y_n} cover K. Set
V=V_{y_1}\cap \cdots \cap V_{y_n}.
Then V is an open neighborhood of x disjoint from U_{y_1}\cup \cdots \cup U_{y_n}, and hence disjoint from K. Every point outside K therefore has an open neighborhood contained in X\setminus K. The complement is open, so K is closed.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Euclidean real line is Hausdorff but noncompact. In the other direction, an infinite cofinite space is compact and connected, yet it is not Hausdorff.

fr:title.text: A Hausdorff Space Need Not Be Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Hausdorff Space Need Not Be Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every Euclidean space \mathbb {R}^n, for n\geq 1, is Hausdorff. Given distinct points x,y, choose \varepsilon =d(x,y)/3. The Euclidean balls B_\varepsilon (x) and B_\varepsilon (y) are disjoint by the triangle inequality, so they separate the two points.

fr:title.text: An Infinite Cofinite Space Is Compact but Not Hausdorff

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An Infinite Cofinite Space Is Compact but Not Hausdorff

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X be infinite and carry the cofinite topology. Given an open cover of X, choose one nonempty member U_0. Its complement is finite. For each of the finitely many points outside U_0, choose one further member of the cover containing that point. Together with U_0, these sets form a finite subcover, so X is compact.

Any two nonempty open subsets of X intersect: the complement of their intersection is a union of two finite sets and cannot be all of the infinite set X. Distinct points therefore cannot have disjoint open neighborhoods. Hence X is not Hausdorff. The same observation shows that X is connected.

Compactness and Hausdorffness become especially effective when they occur on opposite sides of a continuous bijection. Compactness makes closed information survive the map, and Hausdorffness recognizes the image as closed. This supplies a widely used criterion for proving that a bijection is a homeomorphism.
Let f:X\to Y be a continuous bijection. If X is compact and Y is Hausdorff, then f is a homeomorphism.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let C\subseteq X be closed. It is compact by compactness of closed subspaces, and its image f(C) is compact by preservation of compactness. Since Y is Hausdorff, compact subsets are closed, so f(C) is closed in Y. Thus f is a closed map.
For the inverse map f^{-1}:Y\to X, the preimage of a closed set C\subseteq X is
(f^{-1})^{-1}(C)=f(C),
which is closed in Y. Hence f^{-1} is continuous, and f is a homeomorphism.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can now return to the quotient construction. Gluing the two endpoints of a compact interval produces a circle, and the criterion above turns the evident continuous bijection into a homeomorphism.

fr:title.text: The Circle as a Quotient of an Interval

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Circle as a Quotient of an Interval

fr:mainmatter.html:p:
Let
S^1=\{z\in \mathbb {C}\mid |z|=1\}, \qquad q:[0,1]\longrightarrow S^1, \qquad q(t)=e^{2\pi i t}.
The map q identifies precisely the endpoints 0 and 1. Let p:[0,1]\to [0,1]/(0\sim 1) be the canonical quotient map. There is a unique bijection
\bar q:[0,1]/(0\sim 1)\longrightarrow S^1
such that \bar q\circ p=q.

Since q is continuous, the universal property of the quotient makes \bar q continuous. The interval [0,1] is compact by compactness of closed intervals, and its quotient is compact by preservation under continuous images. The circle is Hausdorff as a subspace of the Euclidean plane. Therefore the compact-to-Hausdorff criterion shows that \bar q is a homeomorphism:
[0,1]/(0\sim 1)\cong S^1.

A basis may still be too large for explicit arguments. The two standard countability axioms ask whether local neighborhoods or the entire topology can be controlled by countable data. The second condition is stronger because one global basis must work simultaneously at every point.
A topological space X is first-countable if every point x\in X has an at most countable local basis. It is second-countable if its topology has an at most countable basis.

These conditions constrain two different scales. First-countability gives a countable collection of tests near each individual point, while second-countability gives one countable collection of basic open sets for the whole space.
Every second-countable topological space is first-countable.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Let \mathcal {B} be a countable basis for X. For each x\in X, set
\mathcal {B}_x=\{B\in \mathcal {B}\mid x\in B\}.
This is a countable collection of open neighborhoods of x. If N is any neighborhood of x, choose an open set U with x\in U\subseteq N. The basis property supplies B\in \mathcal {B}_x with x\in B\subseteq U\subseteq N. Therefore \mathcal {B}_x is a countable local basis at x.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Rational endpoints give a countable basis for the Euclidean real line. In contrast, an uncountable discrete space has a one-element local basis at every point but cannot have a countable global basis.

In the Euclidean real line, let
\mathcal {B} =\{(p,q)\mid p,q\in \mathbb {Q},\;p<q\}.
This collection is countable because \mathbb {Q}\times \mathbb {Q} is countable. It is a basis: whenever U is open and x\in U, there is an interval (a,b) with x\in (a,b)\subseteq U; density of the rationals gives p,q\in \mathbb {Q} with
a<p<x<q<b.
Thus x\in (p,q)\subseteq U. Hence \mathbb {R} is second-countable and, by second-countability implies first-countability, also first-countable.

fr:title.text: An Uncountable Discrete Space Is Not Second-Countable

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An Uncountable Discrete Space Is Not Second-Countable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let X be an uncountable set with the discrete topology. For every x\in X, the one-element collection \{\{x\}\} is a local basis at x; hence X is first-countable.

On the other hand, every basis \mathcal {B} for X must contain every singleton. Indeed, since \{x\} is open, the basis property requires some B\in \mathcal {B} with
x\in B\subseteq \{x\},
and therefore B=\{x\}. Thus \mathcal {B} is uncountable, so X is not second-countable. This also shows why the two countability axioms are genuinely different.

First-countability explains why sequences suffice for many arguments in metric spaces. Without such a hypothesis, sequences alone may fail to detect closure or continuity; nets or filters are then the appropriate general substitutes.

A noncompact space may nevertheless look compact around each point. Local compactness records this intermediate situation. It is strong enough to support many constructions from analysis while still including open subsets of Euclidean spaces and manifolds.
A topological space X is locally compact at x\in X if there exists a compact subspace K\subseteq X that is a neighborhood of x. The space is locally compact if it is locally compact at every point.

This definition does not include the Hausdorff condition. In a different convention, some texts use locally compact to mean locally compact and Hausdorff. Outside the Hausdorff setting, several common formulations of local compactness need not be equivalent.

fr:title.text: The Real Line Is Locally Compact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The Real Line Is Locally Compact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For each x\in \mathbb {R}, the closed interval K=[x-1,x+1] is compact by compactness of closed intervals. It contains the open interval (x-1,x+1), so K is a neighborhood of x. Therefore the Euclidean real line is locally compact.

Keeping Hausdorffness separate from local compactness makes the convention explicit. It also prevents equivalent formulations from the Hausdorff setting from being used automatically in spaces where those formulations may diverge.

The concepts above form the basic toolkit of point-set topology. Bases present topologies, continuous maps compare them, subspaces, products, and quotients construct new spaces, and connectedness, compactness, Hausdorffness, countability, and local compactness measure the resulting spaces. Natural next steps include stronger separation axioms, the Tychonoff theorem, metrization theorems, and compactifications.
Every second-countable topological space is first-countable.

Let \mathcal {B} be a countable basis for X. For each x\in X, set
\mathcal {B}_x=\{B\in \mathcal {B}\mid x\in B\}.
This is a countable collection of open neighborhoods of x. If N is any neighborhood of x, choose an open set U with x\in U\subseteq N. The basis property supplies B\in \mathcal {B}_x with x\in B\subseteq U\subseteq N. Therefore \mathcal {B}_x is a countable local basis at x.

Let (X,\tau ) be a topological space. A collection \mathcal {B}\subseteq \tau is a basis for \tau if, whenever U\in \tau and x\in U, there is some B\in \mathcal {B} such that
x\in B\subseteq U.
Equivalently, every open set is a union of members of \mathcal {B}.

A collection \mathcal {B}\subseteq \mathcal {P}(X) generates a topology by taking arbitrary unions of its members provided that it covers X and satisfies the refinement condition
x\in B_1\cap B_2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \exists B_3\in \mathcal {B},\; x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2.

Let X be a topological space and let x\in X. A subset N\subseteq X is a neighborhood of x if there is an open set U such that
x\in U\subseteq N.
In particular, a neighborhood need not itself be open.

A collection \mathcal {B}_x of neighborhoods of x is a local basis at x if every neighborhood N of x contains some B\in \mathcal {B}_x. A statement holds locally at x when it holds on some neighborhood of x.
